title: Growing fennel microgreens
subtitle: Feathery herb microgreens with an anise flavour, cut in 10 to 14 days
excerpt: Fennel microgreens grow as fine, feathery fronds with a clean anise flavour. They take 10 to 14 days on a 25 cm indoor tray and pair well with fish, seafood, and salads. The growing method is straightforward: sow, blackout, then grow in light.
sourceNotes: UMass Extension microgreens guides (open-access). Cornell Cooperative Extension indoor growing material. Standard microgreen-growing practice synthesised from extension service material.

glossaryTerms.definition: Watering by setting the growing tray inside a second tray filled with water, allowing the growing medium to draw moisture up from below. Keeps the seedling surface dry and reduces mould and damping-off risk in microgreen trays.

A fungal condition where seedling stems collapse and rot at the soil surface. Caused by Pythium, Fusarium, and Rhizoctonia species in warm, wet, poorly-ventilated conditions. Common in overcrowded or overwatered microgreen trays.

content.text: Fennel microgreens are a year-round indoor tray crop with a 10 to 14 day cycle. Sow on a pre-dampened seed compost tray, blackout for two to three days, then grow in bright light until the feathery fronds are 5 to 8 cm tall. The anise flavour is clean and assertive; a little goes a long way as a garnish or salad component.
Fennel microgreens pair particularly well with fish, seafood, cucumber, and citrus. The delicate frond texture means they break down in heat; use raw, added after cooking.

Light: a bright south-facing windowsill in spring and summer. A grow light 15 to 20 cm above the tray at 14 to 16 hours per day in winter. Fennel microgreens in low light elongate quickly and the fronds become wispy with weakened flavour.
Temperature: 16 to 22°C. Fennel germinates and grows reliably across this range. It is slightly more tolerant of cool conditions than basil or coriander.

Day 0: sow. Fill the tray with pre-dampened seed compost to within 1 cm of the rim. Scatter fennel seed at 15 to 20 g per 25 cm tray. Fennel seed is light and long; scatter from 15 cm above the surface for even distribution. Press gently into contact with the medium.
Days 1 to 3: blackout. Cover with a second tray, lightly weighted. Fennel germinates in two to three days; remove the cover when the majority of shoots are upright at 2 to 3 cm.
Day 4 onward: light. The feathery fronds develop and green up within 24 to 48 hours.
daily: set the growing tray inside a second tray with 1 to 2 cm of water. Remove excess after 30 minutes.
Days 10 to 14: cut. When the feathery fronds are fully developed and 5 to 8 cm tall, cut 1 cm above the medium surface. Use fresh; fennel microgreens wilt within a few hours of cutting.

attrs.heading: Troubleshooting
attrs.intro: Common problems on fennel microgreen trays.

items.symptom: Slow or uneven germination past day 4
items.cause: Old seed stock or seed buried too deep.
items.fix: Use fresh seed from the current season. Press seed into contact with the medium surface rather than burying it.

items.cause: Too dense a sowing on the tray.
items.fix: Reduce to 10 to 15 g per tray on the next attempt. Some clumping is normal; gently separate with a fork before plating.

items.symptom: Pale, elongated shoots with little flavour
items.fix: Move to a brighter position or add a grow light. Fennel microgreens grown in low light lack both colour and flavour.

content.text: Use untreated fennel seed. Fennel seed sold for culinary use (in spice jars) is usually dried for flavour and may have low viability. Buy from a vegetable seed supplier or microgreen seed supplier. Florence fennel and common fennel both work; the flavour profile is similar.
risk is moderate. Bottom-water only and ensure the room is ventilated. Fennel is less susceptible than basil but still benefits from consistent airflow.
